notions.question: How is a business letter laid out in English?
notions.definition: The English business letter follows a standard layout, nowadays most often “full block” (everything aligned to the left, with no paragraph indentation). Order of elements: the sender's letterhead, the date, the recipient's address (inside address), any reference, the salutation, the subject line, the body of the letter, the complimentary close, the signature, name and job title, and a mention of any enclosures (Enc. / Encl.). The date is preferably written with the month in letters to avoid ambiguity: 15 October 2026 (British) or October 15, 2026 (American); 10/03/2026 means 10 March in the United Kingdom but 3 October in the United States.

etapes: Letterhead (company name, address and contact details)
Inside address: recipient's name, job title, company and address
Salutation: Dear Ms Taylor, / Dear Sir or Madam,
Body: short paragraphs, one idea per paragraph
Complimentary close: Yours sincerely, / Yours faithfully,

termes.definition: Line summarising the purpose of the letter.

termes.fr: Présentation à la française en bloc
termes.definition: All elements aligned to the left.

exemple.texte: Loire Valves SA, 12 rue des Carmes, 45000 Orléans, France — 15 October 2026 — Ms Emma Taylor, Purchasing Manager, Midlands Engineering Ltd, Birmingham B1 1AA, United Kingdom — Dear Ms Taylor, — Re: Your enquiry of 10 October — … — Yours sincerely, — Claire Martin, Export Sales Assistant — Enc. Price list

confusions.explication: Writing the month in letters removes any ambiguity.

verification: In what order should the date, the recipient's address and the subject line be placed?

notions.question: Which complimentary close should you choose depending on the salutation?
notions.definition: In British English, the complimentary close depends on the salutation: if you do not know the recipient's name (Dear Sir or Madam, Dear Sirs), you end with “Yours faithfully”; if you do (Dear Mr Brown, Dear Ms Lee), with “Yours sincerely”. In American English, “Sincerely” or “Sincerely yours” is used in both cases, and the salutation is followed by a colon (Dear Mr. Brown:). In an e-mail or an established relationship: “Kind regards”, “Best regards”, “Best wishes”. “Ms” is the neutral form for a woman when her marital status is unknown, or as standard professional usage.

lignes: Dear Mr Smith, / Dear Ms Jones,

fonctionnement.texte: A French-style closing formula (« Je vous prie d'agréer… ») is not translated: replace it with a forward-looking sentence (“We look forward to hearing from you.”) followed by the standard close.

termes.definition: Form of address at the top of a letter.

exemple.texte: “Dear Sir or Madam, We would be grateful if you could send us your latest catalogue. We look forward to hearing from you. Yours faithfully, …”

confusions.explication: A classic British rule, still expected in formal writing.

verification: Which close should you use for a letter beginning “Dear Ms Patel”?

notions.question: How can you be polite and nuanced in business English without being too direct?
notions.definition: The English professional register favours courtesy and softening (hedging): requests are phrased indirectly (Could you…? We would be grateful if…), bad news is softened (Unfortunately, We regret to inform you that…), direct criticism is avoided (It appears that… rather than You made a mistake), and positive phrasing is preferred. The style remains clear and concise (plain English): short sentences, active verbs, no unnecessary jargon. Contractions (we're, don't) are reserved for less formal e-mails.

lignes: Could you please send us the invoice?
It appears that the shipment has not yet arrived.
We would appreciate it if you could consider a discount.
I'm afraid we are unable to accept these terms.
We have experienced some problems with the product.

termes.definition: Level of language used in official writing.

exemple.texte: Instead of “You have not paid invoice 2041”, write: “According to our records, invoice No. 2041 of 15 August remains unpaid. We would be grateful if you could look into this matter.”

confusions.b: French formulas translated word for word
confusions.explication: Long French formulas sound heavy in English: prefer courteous concision.

verification: Rephrase politely: “Give us a better price.”

notions.question: How do you write a request for information or a quotation to a foreign supplier?
notions.definition: The enquiry (British spelling; inquiry in American English) opens the business cycle. It includes: the source of the contact (how you know of the supplier), a brief presentation of your company, the precise request (catalogue, prices, terms of payment and delivery, lead times, quantity discounts, samples), a possible prospect of an order, and a closing formula. It remains concise and precise in order to obtain a usable reply.

lignes: We saw your stand at… / Your name was given to us by…
We are a leading importer of… based in…
Could you please send us your current price list and details of your terms of payment and delivery?
We would also like to know whether you offer quantity discounts / can deliver by…
If your prices are competitive, we may place a substantial order.
We look forward to hearing from you.

termes.definition: Reduction granted for a large order.
Specimen of the product for testing.

exemple.texte: “Dear Sir or Madam, We visited your stand at the Frankfurt Ambiente fair and were impressed by your range of ceramic tableware. We are a chain of 25 kitchenware shops in France. Could you please send us your export price list, together with your terms of payment and delivery times to Orléans? We would also like to know whether you grant quantity discounts. We look forward to hearing from you. Yours faithfully, …”

confusions.explication: An enquiry does not commit the buyer.

verification: What information should you ask for in an export enquiry?

notions.question: How do you reply to an enquiry with an offer or a quotation in English?
notions.definition: The reply to an enquiry thanks the sender for the request and presents the offer or quotation (estimate for an approximate amount): products, unit prices and currency, Incoterm and place, terms of payment, delivery time, discounts, period of validity of the offer, enclosed documents (catalogue, pro forma invoice). It highlights the offer and encourages an order. Legally, a “firm” offer is binding for its period of validity; the phrases “subject to availability” or “without engagement” limit the commitment.

lignes: Thank you for your enquiry of 10 October.
We are pleased to quote as follows: … at €12.50 per unit, FCA Orléans (Incoterms® 2020).
Our terms are payment by bank transfer within 30 days of invoice date.
Delivery can be made within four weeks of receipt of order.
This offer is valid until 30 November 2026.
We are confident that our products will meet your requirements.

termes.definition: Preliminary invoice serving as an offer or as a document for the buyer.
Offer binding the seller during its period of validity.

exemple.texte: “Thank you for your enquiry of 10 October. We are pleased to quote €12.50 per piece for our Vienna dinner plates, FCA Orléans (Incoterms® 2020), for a minimum order of 1,000 pieces. We offer a 5% discount on orders over 5,000 pieces. Payment: 30 days net. This offer is valid until 30 November 2026.”

confusions.explication: An estimate is indicative; a quotation gives a precise figure.

verification: Why should a quotation state the Incoterm and its version?

notions.question: How do you place and confirm an order in English?
notions.definition: The order, often accompanied by a purchase order (PO), accurately restates the offer reference, the items (references, quantities, prices), the Incoterm, the terms of payment, the date and place of delivery, the packing, marking and shipping instructions, and the documents required. The supplier acknowledges receipt (acknowledgement of order), confirms the terms or points out any change (which may amount to a counter-offer) and states the expected shipping date.

lignes: Please find enclosed our order No. 785 for… / We are pleased to place an order for…
Please mark each case… / The goods should be shipped by sea to…
Thank you for your order No. 785, which we are pleased to confirm.
We regret that item 4 is out of stock; we can offer a similar model at…
The goods will be dispatched on… We will send you the shipping documents as soon as…

termes.es: orden de compra / nota de pedido
acuse de recibo / confirmación de pedido

exemple.texte: “Thank you for your quotation of 15 October. Please find enclosed our order No. PO-785 for 3,000 Vienna dinner plates at €12.50 each, FCA Orléans (Incoterms® 2020). Please pack the plates in cartons of 24 and mark them as shown on the attached sheet. Delivery is required by 15 December 2026.”

confusions.a: Ship (to send, whatever the mode of transport)
confusions.explication: “To ship” is also used for consignments sent by road or air.

verification: Why must the acknowledgement point out any change?

notions.question: How do you make a complaint and reply to one in English?
notions.definition: The letter of complaint sets out the facts precisely and without aggressiveness: order reference, the problem found (goods damaged, wrong items, short delivery, late delivery), the consequences, a precise request (replacement, refund, credit note, discount) and a deadline. The reply (adjustment letter) thanks the customer, apologises if the complaint is justified, briefly explains the cause without over-justifying, offers a concrete solution and gives reassurance about the future; if the complaint is unjustified, it declines tactfully and with arguments.

lignes: We are writing to inform you that… / We regret to say that…
Thank you for your letter of… concerning…
On opening the cases, we found that 12 plates were broken.
We apologise for the inconvenience caused.
We must ask you to replace the damaged goods.
We will send replacements immediately at our expense.
We would appreciate a prompt reply.
We have taken steps to ensure this does not happen again.

termes.definition: Quantity delivered lower than the quantity ordered.

exemple.texte: “We are writing about order No. PO-785, delivered on 12 December. On inspection, we found that 120 plates were chipped, owing to inadequate packing. We would be grateful if you could send replacements by the end of the month or issue a credit note for €1,500.”

confusions.explication: “Claim” is more legal or insurance-related; “complaint” is more general.

verification: What are the steps of a good reply to a justified complaint?

notions.question: How do you chase a customer who has not paid without damaging the relationship?
notions.definition: Reminders follow a gradation: the first reminder is courteous and assumes an oversight; the second reminder is firmer, refers to the first and asks for an explanation; the final demand sets a deadline and announces the measures envisaged (suspension of deliveries, late-payment interest, debt collection, legal action). The invoice is enclosed or referred to (invoice number, amount, due date) and payment is made easy (bank details).

lignes: We would like to remind you that invoice No. 2041 for €8,400 was due on 15 September. Perhaps it has been overlooked.
We have not yet received payment despite our letter of… Please let us know if there is any problem.
Unless payment is received within 10 days, we shall be obliged to place the matter in the hands of our solicitors.

termes.definition: Letter reminding the customer of a due date.
Last request before action is taken.

exemple.texte: “Dear Mr Brown, According to our records, invoice No. 2041 dated 15 August for €8,400 remains outstanding. We would be grateful if you could settle this amount at your earliest convenience. If you have already made the payment, please disregard this letter. Yours sincerely, …”

confusions.explication: In a financial context the meaning is “unsettled”.

verification: What is the difference in tone between the first reminder and the final demand?

notions.question: How does a professional e-mail differ from a letter?
notions.definition: A professional e-mail is shorter and often less formal than a letter, but it must still be carefully written. Good practice: a precise, informative subject line; an appropriate salutation (Dear Mr Smith, / Hi John, depending on the relationship); the main message in the first sentence; short paragraphs; a clear request with a deadline; a closing formula (Best regards, Kind regards) and a full signature. Avoid capital letters (perceived as shouting), humour and irony, and informal abbreviations, and check recipients, attachments and tone before sending.

lignes: I am writing to let you know that…
Could you confirm by Friday 20 November whether…?
Please find attached the revised schedule.
Let me know if you have any questions. Best regards,

exemple.texte: Subject: PO-785 – shipment delayed to 18 December. “Dear Ms Taylor, I am writing to inform you that, owing to a production issue, order PO-785 will be shipped on 18 December instead of 15 December. We apologise for any inconvenience. Could you let me know by Friday whether this new date suits you? Best regards, Claire Martin”

confusions.explication: “Attached” for an attached file, “enclosed” for a paper document.

verification: Name four rules for writing an effective professional e-mail.

questions.enonce: Why write “3 October 2026” rather than “03/10/2026” in a letter to an American customer?

choix.texte: Because in the United States 03/10/2026 is read as 10 March
Because it is a legal requirement

questions.enonce: A British letter begins “Dear Sir or Madam”. Which close should you choose?
Which wording is the most appropriate for informing a supplier of a delay?

choix.texte: “It appears that the goods have not yet arrived. Could you please look into this?”

questions.enonce: “Enquiry” translates into French as:

choix.explication: A possible meaning elsewhere (police investigation), but not in business correspondence.

questions.enonce: Which elements must an export quotation specify?

choix.texte: The unit price and the currency

questions.enonce: In French, “purchase order” means:
Which sentence is appropriate for requesting a credit note?

choix.texte: “We would be grateful if you could issue a credit note for the damaged items.”

questions.enonce: Which sentence belongs in a final demand?

choix.texte: “Unless payment is received within ten days, we shall take legal action.”
“We look forward to doing business with you.”

questions.enonce: True or false: in a professional e-mail, you write “Please find attached” for an attached file.

choix.explication: “Enclosed” is used for a paper document.

flashcards.question: Present the layout of a business letter, salutations and complimentary closes, and the rules of register.
flashcards.reponse: Full block: letterhead, date (15 October 2026 / October 15, 2026), inside address, salutation, subject line (Re:), body, complimentary close, signature, Enc. Dear Sir or Madam → Yours faithfully; Dear Ms Lee → Yours sincerely; US: Sincerely; e-mail: Kind/Best regards. Register: courtesy and softening (Could you…, We would be grateful if…, It appears that…, Unfortunately…), plain English, short sentences; no literal translation of French formulas.

flashcards.question: Describe the cycle of business correspondence in English with a key phrase for each stage.
flashcards.reponse: Enquiry: Could you please send us your price list and terms? Offer/quotation: We are pleased to quote… FCA Orléans (Incoterms® 2020), valid until… Order: Please find enclosed our order No… Acknowledgement: Thank you for your order, which we are pleased to confirm. Complaint: On opening the cases, we found that… We would be grateful if you could replace… Reply: We apologise for the inconvenience. Reminder: Invoice No… remains outstanding; final demand: Unless payment is received within…
indispensables: Vocabulary: quotation, purchase order, credit note, outstanding

exercices.titre: Writing a letter of complaint in English
exercices.enonce: On 12 December your company (Loire Kitchenware, Orléans) received order PO-785 from Midlands Ceramics Ltd (Stoke-on-Trent): 3,000 plates, 120 of which were chipped because of inadequate packing. You request replacement before the end of the month or, failing that, a credit note for €1,500. Recipient: Ms Emma Taylor, Sales Manager.

questions.consigne: Write the letter (body, salutation and complimentary close).

criteres: Salutation “Dear Ms Taylor,” and close “Yours sincerely,”
Subject line with the order reference
Clear request with a deadline and an alternative solution (credit note)
Courteous, softened tone; accurate vocabulary (chipped, packing, replacement, credit note)
reponse.corrige:
Dear Ms Taylor,

Re: Order No. PO-785

We received the above order on 12 December. Unfortunately, on unpacking the cartons, we found that 120 of the 3,000 plates were chipped, apparently because of inadequate packing.

We would be grateful if you could send replacements by 31 December, as we need the plates for our January promotion. Should this not be possible, we would ask you to issue a credit note for €1,500.

We look forward to your prompt reply.

Yours sincerely,

Claire Martin
Purchasing Assistant, Loire Kitchenware

notions.question: How do you refer to the legal forms, functions and organisation of a company in English?
notions.definition: Company vocabulary covers legal forms (sole trader, partnership, private limited company “Ltd” in the United Kingdom, public limited company “plc”, which may be listed, corporation “Inc.” in the United States, limited liability company “LLC”), governing bodies and positions (board of directors, chair, chief executive officer “CEO”, managing director “MD” in the United Kingdom, chief financial officer “CFO”), departments (sales, purchasing, human resources, accounts, logistics) and stakeholders (shareholders, stakeholders, employees / staff, suppliers, customers).

fonctionnement.texte: Equivalences between company forms are approximate: keep the original term and add an explanation (“SAS, a French simplified joint-stock company”).

termes.definition: Party affected by the company's activity.

exemple.texte: “Loire Valves SAS, a French company with a workforce of 120, is a subsidiary of a German group. Its managing director reports to the group's board. Turnover reached €35 million last year, 60% of which was generated abroad.”

confusions.explication: Context decides; “staff turnover” refers to the rate at which employees are replaced.

verification: Translate: « le siège social », « l'actionnaire », « le conseil d'administration ».

notions.question: How do you read a balance sheet and an income statement in English?
notions.definition: Financial statements comprise the balance sheet (or statement of financial position under IFRS), the income statement (profit and loss account, P&L) and the cash flow statement. Key terms: assets (current / non-current), liabilities, equity, revenue, cost of sales, gross profit, operating profit, EBITDA (close to the French EBE), net profit / net income, depreciation (of tangible fixed assets), amortisation (of intangible assets), accounts receivable (amounts owed by customers), accounts payable (amounts owed to suppliers), cash flow, dividend.

lignes: income statement / profit and loss account (P&L)
net profit / net income / bottom line

termes.definition: Statement of a company's assets and liabilities at a given date.

termes.es: cuenta de resultados / de pérdidas y ganancias

termes.definition: Share of profit distributed to shareholders.

exemple.texte: “Revenue rose by 8% to €35m, while operating profit fell slightly owing to higher energy costs. Net income stood at €2.1m. Trade receivables increased, putting pressure on cash flow.”

confusions.explication: Partial false friend: French « dépréciation » is impairment in English.

verification: How do you translate « créances clients » and « dettes fournisseurs » into British English?

notions.question: Which English terms do you need to master to follow an import-export transaction?
notions.definition: International trade is largely conducted in English: rules and documents (Incoterms, commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading “B/L”, air waybill “AWB”, CMR consignment note, certificate of origin, letter of credit “L/C”, documentary collection), actors (freight forwarder, carrier, shipping line, customs broker, consignee, shipper, issuing / confirming bank), operations (to ship, shipment, consignment, customs clearance, duty, tariff, quota, warehouse, container “TEU”, lead time, tracking).

termes.definition: Organises transport on behalf of the shipper.
Person to whom the goods are delivered.

exemple.texte: “The goods will be shipped FOB Le Havre (Incoterms® 2020). Our freight forwarder will send you a copy of the bill of lading, the commercial invoice and the packing list. Payment is to be made by irrevocable letter of credit confirmed by a French bank.”

confusions.explication: Two different actors in maritime transport.

verification: Translate: « transitaire », « connaissement », « dédouanement ».

notions.question: How do you talk about markets, products and communication in English?
notions.definition: Key terms: market research, target market / segment, positioning, brand / branding, market share, the marketing mix (4 Ps: product, price, place, promotion), distribution channel, retailer / wholesaler, point of sale, advertising campaign, social media marketing, customer loyalty, customer relationship management (CRM), launch, competitive advantage, unique selling point (USP), pricing strategy (penetration / skimming pricing).

termes.definition: Proportion of a market's sales achieved by a company.
The public's perception of the brand.
Paid communication intended to promote something.

exemple.texte: “Our target market is urban consumers aged 25 to 40. We plan to launch the product in Spain next spring with a social media campaign, aiming for a 3% market share within two years.”

confusions.b: An advertisement / an ad (a single ad)
confusions.explication: You cannot say “an advertising”.

verification: What do “USP” and “market share” mean?

notions.question: Which terms help you understand economic news in English?
notions.definition: Macroeconomic and current-affairs terms: GDP (gross domestic product), growth, recession, inflation, deflation, unemployment rate, interest rate, central bank (the Bank of England, the Federal Reserve “Fed”, the European Central Bank “ECB”), monetary / fiscal policy, budget deficit, public debt, trade balance (surplus / deficit), exchange rate, tariffs, free trade agreement, supply chain, consumer spending, investment, productivity, labour market (UK) / labor market (US).

lignes: key interest rate / policy rate / base rate (UK)

termes.definition: Decline in economic activity (often two consecutive quarters of falling GDP).
Government action through spending and taxation.

exemple.texte: “The central bank raised its key interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to curb inflation, while GDP growth slowed to 0.8%.”

confusions.explication: False friend: “fiscal” concerns the government budget as a whole.

verification: Translate: « politique budgétaire », « taux directeur », « déficit commercial ».

notions.question: Which English words look like French words but have a different meaning?
notions.definition: False friends are words that look similar but have different meanings in the two languages. In business English, they frequently cause mistranslations: actually (« en fait », not « actuellement » → currently), eventually (« finalement », not « éventuellement » → possibly), to control (to manage, to master, rather than « contrôler » → to check), library (« bibliothèque », not « librairie » → bookshop), sensible (« raisonnable », not « sensible » → sensitive), to pretend (« faire semblant », not « prétendre » → to claim), agenda (« ordre du jour »), formation (≠ training, « formation professionnelle »), fabric (« tissu », ≠ factory), to assist (« aider », ≠ to attend: « assister à »), commodity (« matière première, produit de base »).

lignes: to be present at (a meeting) (« assister à »)
list of items for a meeting (« ordre du jour »)

termes.definition: Word that looks similar but has a different meaning.

exemple.texte: “We will eventually open an office in Madrid” means « Nous finirons par ouvrir un bureau à Madrid », not « éventuellement ».

confusions.explication: “To attend” = to be present at, to take part in (« assister à »).

verification: Translate correctly: « actuellement », « éventuellement », « une usine ».

notions.question: How do you write and comment on figures and changes in English?
notions.definition: English uses the decimal point and the comma as the thousands separator (1,250.5 = French 1 250,5). “A billion” is 10⁹ (French « milliard »), “a trillion” a thousand billion. Distinguish “per cent” (percentage) from “percentage point”: a rate that goes from 4% to 5% rises by one percentage point, i.e. by 25%. Trend verbs: to rise / increase / grow (upward), to fall / decrease / decline / drop (downward), to soar / rocket (sharp rise), to plummet / slump (sharp fall), to level off / stabilise (stabilisation), to peak (reach a high point), to fluctuate. Prepositions: rise by (the difference) / rise to (the level reached) / from … to.

termes.definition: Unit measuring the difference between two percentages.

exemple.texte: “Exports rose by 12% to €4.5 billion in 2025, while the unemployment rate fell by 0.4 percentage points to 7.1%.”

confusions.explication: A classic trap between English and Spanish.
“Sales rose by 10%” ≠ “Sales rose to 10%”.

verification: A rate goes from 2% to 3%: by how many points and by what percentage has it increased?

flashcards.reponse: Actually = « en fait »; eventually = « finalement »; sensible = « raisonnable »; to attend = « assister à »; fabric = « tissu »; library = « bibliothèque »; commodity = « matière première »; fiscal policy = « politique budgétaire ». notions.titre: Reading a business article in English
notions.question: How can you understand an article from the English-language business press quickly and accurately?
notions.definition: Efficient reading combines several passes: skimming the headline, the standfirst, the subheadings and the first sentence of each paragraph to grasp the topic; scanning for specific figures, names and dates; then detailed reading to understand the line of argument (thesis, arguments, examples, quoted opinions). You need to identify the source (newspaper, date, editorial stance), distinguish facts from opinions, spot logical connectors (however, therefore, whereas, despite) and expert quotations, and note new vocabulary in its context.

etapes: Identify the source, the date and the type of article (news, analysis, op-ed)
Skimming: headline, standfirst, subheadings, first sentences
Detailed reading: main idea of each paragraph, logical links
Distinguish facts, the author's opinions and quoted opinions
Summarise the article in three sentences

termes.definition: Fast reading to grasp the general idea.
Searching for specific pieces of information.

exemple.texte: Headline: “Car makers brace for tariff hit”. Skimming: car makers are preparing for the impact of new tariffs. Scanning: 25% tariffs, coming into force in March, three car makers mentioned. Detailed reading: the author contrasts the manufacturers' arguments (higher prices) with the government's (reshoring).

confusions.explication: The verbs “claim”, “argue” and “warn” signal an attributed opinion.

verification: What is the difference between skimming and scanning?

notions.question: How do you write a synthesis of several documents in English?
notions.definition: A summary or synthesis in English gives an objective, organised account of the ideas in one or more documents, in your own words and within a set length. You begin with an introductory sentence that situates the documents and the topic (“The documents deal with…”), organise the ideas by theme while comparing the sources (“Both articles point out that… whereas…”), rephrase rather than copy, use precise reporting verbs (state, argue, claim, point out, warn, highlight), and end with a brief conclusion without any personal opinion, unless instructed otherwise.

lignes: The three documents deal with / focus on…
According to…, the author argues / points out / warns that…
Both documents agree that… / Unlike document 1, document 2…
However, … / whereas… / on the other hand…
All in all, the documents show that…

termes.definition: Verb used to report what someone else said.

exemple.texte: “The two articles deal with the rise of nearshoring in Europe. Both point out that companies are moving production closer to home to secure supply chains. However, while the first article highlights job creation in Eastern Europe, the second warns that higher labour costs may reduce competitiveness.”

confusions.explication: Rephrasing is required.

verification: Name four reporting verbs and their nuance.

questions.enonce: Quickly locating all the figures in an article is called:

choix.explication: Fast reading for the general idea.

questions.enonce: “The minister claimed that the reform would create 50,000 jobs.” What does the verb “claimed” tell you?

choix.texte: It is the minister's assertion, which the journalist does not endorse

questions.enonce: Which practices are appropriate in a synthesis written in English?

choix.texte: Comparing the documents theme by theme
Adding your personal opinion in every paragraph
choix.explication: Objectivity is required, unless instructed otherwise.

choix.texte: Using a variety of reporting verbs

flashcards.question: Describe the method for reading a business article in English and the method for writing a synthesis.
flashcards.reponse: Reading: source and type of article, skimming (headline, standfirst, subheadings, first sentences), scanning (figures, actors, dates), detailed reading (ideas, logical links), distinguishing facts from opinions (claim, argue, warn). Synthesis: an introduction situating the documents, a thematic structure comparing the sources (both… whereas… unlike…), rephrasing, reporting verbs, a brief conclusion, no personal opinion unless instructed, length respected.
erreurs: Summarising the documents one after the other

notions.question: How do you express obligation, possibility or politeness with English modal verbs?
notions.definition: Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would) are followed by the bare infinitive without “to”, take no -s in the third person and form the negative and the interrogative on their own. They express degrees of possibility (may, might, could), obligation (must; have to for an external obligation; “mustn't” = prohibition, “don't have to” = absence of obligation), advice (should), ability (can, could), polite requests (could you, would you), willingness or the future (will, would). In business correspondence, could and would soften requests; shall expresses obligation in contracts.

lignes: Could you send us a sample?
Invoices must be paid within 30 days.
You don't have to pay a deposit.
The Seller shall deliver the goods.

exemple.texte: “We would be grateful if you could confirm the order. The goods must be delivered by 15 December. You don't have to sign the delivery note in person.”

confusions.explication: A common misinterpretation among French speakers.

verification: Translate: « Vous n'êtes pas obligé de payer d'acompte » and « Vous ne devez pas divulguer le prix ».

notions.question: When and how should you use the passive in professional English?
notions.definition: The passive is formed with be conjugated in the required tense + past participle (The goods were shipped). It puts the emphasis on the action or its result rather than on the agent, which is introduced by “by” if it is mentioned. It is frequent in professional and technical writing (processes, reports, procedures) and makes it possible to avoid assigning blame (“Mistakes were made”). English also allows the passive with an indirect object turned into the subject (“We were sent the wrong items”), where French often uses « on ».

termes.definition: Construction in which the subject undergoes the action.
The doer of the action in a passive sentence.

exemple.texte: “Your order has been received and will be processed within 48 hours. You will be informed as soon as the goods are dispatched.”

confusions.explication: English makes the recipient the subject of the passive.

verification: Put into the passive: “We will deliver the goods next week.”

notions.question: How do you express a condition and its consequences in English?
notions.definition: English distinguishes several types of conditional sentences. Type 1 (real / likely): if + present, will + base form (If you order 500 units, we will give you a 5% discount). Type 2 (hypothetical): if + simple past, would + base form (If we lowered our prices, we would sell more). Type 3 (unreal past): if + past perfect, would have + past participle (If you had paid on time, we would have delivered). Unlike French, “will” and “would” are never used in the clause introduced by “if” (except polite “would”: If you would kindly…). “Should you need” is an elegant replacement for “if you need”. Unless = except if.

exemple.texte: “If you confirm your order by Friday, we will ship it on Monday. Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact us. Unless payment is received within ten days, we shall suspend deliveries.”

confusions.explication: No will in the if-clause (except in special cases).

verification: Complete: “If we ___ (receive) your payment, we ___ (ship) the goods.”

notions.question: When should you use the present perfect rather than the simple past?
notions.definition: The simple past places an action in a finished, dated past (We shipped the goods last week / in 2024 / on Monday). The present perfect (have + past participle) links the past to the present: a present result, a review up to now, a duration that continues (We have received your order; Sales have risen this year; We have worked with them since 2015 / for ten years). The markers “yesterday, last, ago, in 2020” call for the simple past; “since, for (ongoing duration), already, yet, so far, recently, this year” call for the present perfect. The French passé composé can therefore be translated by either tense.

exemple.texte: « Nous travaillons avec eux depuis 2018 » → “We have worked (have been working) with them since 2018”, not “We work with them since 2018”.

confusions.explication: A common mistake among French speakers.

verification: Translate: « Les ventes ont augmenté l'an dernier » and « Les ventes ont augmenté cette année ».

questions.enonce: “You don't have to sign the form” means:

choix.texte: There is no obligation for you to sign the form
You are forbidden to sign the form

questions.enonce: Put into the passive: “The forwarder has booked the container.”

choix.texte: The container has been booked by the forwarder.
choix.explication: Present perfect passive: has been + past participle.

choix.texte: The container was booked by the forwarder.
The container has booked by the forwarder.
The container is booking by the forwarder.

questions.enonce: Choose the correct sentence:

choix.texte: If you order 1,000 units, we will offer a discount.
choix.explication: Type 1: if + present, will + base form.

choix.texte: If you will order 1,000 units, we will offer a discount.
If you ordered 1,000 units, we will offer a discount.
If you order 1,000 units, we would offered a discount.

questions.enonce: Translate: « Nous sommes partenaires depuis cinq ans. »

choix.texte: We have been partners for five years.
choix.explication: Present perfect + for (duration up to now).

choix.texte: We are partners since five years.
We were partners for five years.
choix.explication: Implies that the partnership is over.

choix.texte: We have been partners since five years.
choix.explication: Since is used with a starting point (since 2021).

questions.enonce: Which sentence is correct?

choix.texte: We have received your payment yesterday.
choix.explication: Yesterday rules out the present perfect.

flashcards.question: Summarise the useful rules for business English: modals, the passive, conditionals, present perfect / simple past.
flashcards.reponse: Modals + bare infinitive: could/would (politeness), must (obligation), mustn't (prohibition) ≠ don't have to (no obligation), should (advice), may/might (possibility), shall (contractual obligation). Passive: be + past participle, emphasis on the action (Your order has been received). Conditionals: type 1 if + present / will; type 2 if + simple past / would; type 3 if + past perfect / would have; no will after if; should you…, unless. Simple past for the dated past (yesterday, ago, last); present perfect for a link with the present (since, for, yet, already, this year).
indispensables: Simple past and present perfect markers

synthese.essentiel: Four skills: write the business correspondence cycle (enquiry, offer, order, complaint, reminder, e-mail) with the right layout, formulas and softened register; master core company, finance, trade, marketing and economics vocabulary, false friends and numbers; read a press article and write a synthesis in your own words; use the grammar that business English relies on (modals, passive, conditionals, present perfect).

chapitres.idee: Every business letter follows a fixed full-block layout and a courteous, softened register; each stage of the trade cycle has its own key phrases.
points: Layout: letterhead, date, inside address, reference, salutation, subject line (Re:), body, close, signature + job title, Enc.
Date with the month in letters: 15 October 2026 (UK) / October 15, 2026 (US); 10/03/2026 = 10 March UK but 3 October US
Softening: Could you...? We would be grateful if... It appears that... Unfortunately... I'm afraid we are unable to...
Cycle: enquiry -> offer/quotation -> order + acknowledgement -> complaint + adjustment -> reminders
Offer: price, currency, Incoterm and place, payment, delivery, discounts, validity ('This offer is valid until...')
Reminders escalate: courteous (oversight) -> firm (refers to first) -> final demand (deadline + measures)
E-mail: precise subject line, main message first, clear request + deadline, Best/Kind regards; no capitals, no irony
formules: Dear Sir or Madam, ... Yours faithfully, (name unknown)
Dear Ms Lee, ... Yours sincerely, (name known); US: Sincerely, + 'Dear Mr. Brown:'
We look forward to hearing from you. (replaces 'Je vous prie d'agréer...')
Unless payment is received within 10 days, we shall be obliged to place the matter in the hands of our solicitors.

distinctions.difference: Recipient unknown (Dear Sir or Madam) vs named recipient (Dear Ms Jones).
Exact price vs approximate, indicative figure.
A request for information does not commit the buyer; an order is firm.

chapitres.memo: Faithfully goes with the faceless 'Sir or Madam'; sincerely with a name.

questions.q: Rewrite 'You have not paid invoice 2041' politely.
questions.r: According to our records, invoice No. 2041 remains unpaid. We would be grateful if you could look into this matter.
Source of contact, brief company presentation, precise request (prices, terms, lead times, discounts, samples), prospect of an order, closing formula.

questions.q: Structure of a reply to a justified complaint?
questions.r: Thank, apologise, briefly explain the cause, offer a concrete solution (replacement, credit note), reassure about the future.

questions.q: What limits a firm offer's commitment?
questions.r: 'Subject to availability' or 'without engagement'; a firm offer is binding for its validity period.

chapitres.idee: Know the core terms of company, finance, trade, marketing and economics, avoid false friends and write numbers and trends the English way.
points: Company: Ltd (private), plc (public, may be listed), Inc./LLC (US); board of directors, CEO, MD (UK); shareholder, stakeholder, subsidiary
Finance: balance sheet, income statement / P&L, assets, liabilities, equity, accounts receivable/payable, net profit / net income
Trade: freight forwarder, carrier, shipper/consignee, bill of lading (B/L), air waybill, packing list, customs clearance, letter of credit
Marketing: market share, target market, 4 Ps (product, price, place, promotion), USP, skimming / penetration pricing
Economics: GDP, fiscal policy (= budget), monetary policy, key interest rate, trade surplus, supply chain
Numbers: 1,250.50 (decimal point, comma for thousands); billion = milliard; rise BY (difference) / rise TO (level)
Trends: soar/rocket (sharp rise), plummet/slump (sharp fall), level off, peak, fluctuate

distinctions.difference: The activity vs a single ad; never 'an advertising'.
Chiffre d'affaires (UK) vs rotation du personnel.

chapitres.memo: False friends: actually = en fait, eventually = finalement, sensible = raisonnable, to attend = assister à, library = bibliothèque.

questions.q: Translate: chiffre d'affaires, actionnaire, bilan, transitaire, connaissement.
questions.r: Turnover (UK) / revenue (US), shareholder, balance sheet, freight forwarder, bill of lading.
Politique budgétaire (government budget), not politique fiscale (tax policy).

questions.q: Correct: 'Sales rose to 10%' vs 'Sales rose by 10%'.
questions.r: By = the size of the change; to = the level reached.

chapitres.idee: Read in passes (skim, scan, detailed) to separate facts from opinions, then summarise objectively in your own words with reporting verbs.
points: Identify source, date, type (news, analysis, op-ed) and editorial stance
Skimming: headline, standfirst, subheadings, first sentence of each paragraph
Scanning: figures, names, places, dates; then detailed reading of arguments and logical connectors
Claim, argue, warn signal an attributed opinion, not a fact
Synthesis: intro sentence ('The documents deal with...'), thematic plan comparing sources, rephrase, brief conclusion
No personal opinion unless instructed; respect the length
formules: Both documents agree that... / Unlike document 1, document 2...
According to..., the author argues / points out / warns that...
All in all, the documents show that...

distinctions.difference: Survey for the general topic vs search for specific data.

questions.q: What do you read when skimming?
questions.r: Headline, standfirst, subheadings, first sentence of each paragraph.

questions.q: Three rules of a synthesis in English?
questions.r: Thematic structure comparing sources, rephrasing (no copying), no personal opinion unless asked.
State, argue, claim, point out (also warn, highlight).

chapitres.idee: Four structures carry business English: modals for politeness and obligation, the passive for processes, conditionals for terms, and the present perfect / simple past contrast.
points: Modals + bare infinitive, no -s: could/would (polite request), must (obligation), should (advice), may/might (possibility), shall (contract)
Passive = be (in the tense) + past participle: 'Your order has been received'; agent with by
'On nous a envoyé' = 'We were sent' (recipient becomes subject)
Type 1: if + present, will; Type 2: if + past, would; Type 3: if + past perfect, would have + pp
Never will/would in the if-clause; 'Should you need...' = elegant if; unless = except if
Simple past with yesterday, ago, last, in 2020; present perfect with since, for, yet, already, so far, this year
formules: If you order 500 units, we will give you a 5% discount.
We have worked with them since 2018 (not 'We work with them since 2018').

distinctions.difference: Finished, dated past vs link with the present (result, ongoing duration, review).

questions.q: 'You mustn't sign' vs 'You don't have to sign'?
questions.r: Forbidden to sign vs no need to sign.
We have worked / have been working with them since 2018.

questions.q: Correct 'If you will order by Friday, we ship Monday'.
questions.r: If you order by Friday, we will ship on Monday.

parCoeur: Dear Sir or Madam -> Yours faithfully; Dear Ms X -> Yours sincerely; US: Sincerely
Letter order: letterhead, date, inside address, salutation, Re:, body, close, signature, Enc.
We would be grateful if you could... / Could you please...? / We look forward to hearing from you.
Cycle: enquiry, quotation, order, acknowledgement, complaint, adjustment, reminder, final demand
Ltd = private, plc = public; turnover (UK) = revenue (US); shareholder vs stakeholder
Balance sheet, income statement (P&L), assets, liabilities, equity, receivables, payables
Freight forwarder, carrier, shipper, consignee, B/L, AWB, packing list, customs clearance, L/C
False friends: actually, eventually, sensible, to attend, library, fabric, commodity, fiscal
1,250.50; billion = milliard; rise by / rise to; percentage point vs per cent
Conditionals: if + present / will; if + past / would; if + past perfect / would have
Since/for/yet/already -> present perfect; ago/last/yesterday -> simple past
pieges: Ending 'Dear Sir or Madam' with 'Yours sincerely' (should be 'Yours faithfully').
Translating French closing formulas word for word instead of a forward-looking sentence + standard close.
Writing the date in figures only (10/03/2026 is ambiguous between UK and US).
Confusing mustn't (prohibition) with don't have to (no obligation).
Using will in the if-clause, or the present simple with since ('We work here since 2018').
Taking actually, eventually, fiscal or sensible at face value (false friends).
